title: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
summary: How AlphaZero, STaR, ReST-EM, SPIN, Self-Rewarding, V-STaR, Absolute Zero, R-Zero and AlphaProof turn a model's own samples into training data, and what each loop's judge limits.

lessons.title: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill

blocks.md: From the prerequisite courses you know two facts that seem to clash. RLVR with GRPO improves a model using rewards from an automatic checker. Model collapse shows that a model trained again and again on its own samples loses information, starting with rare cases. This course is about loops where a model does generate its own training data and still gets better. The central question for every method: **where does the new information come from?**

Every working loop has the same two steps. An **improvement operator** turns the current model into a stronger but slower or more expensive policy: a tree search, many samples filtered by a checker, or a judge that ranks answers. Then **distillation** trains the fast model to imitate that stronger policy. The improved model makes the operator stronger next round.

Anthony et al. (2017) named this **Expert Iteration** (ExIt): an *apprentice* (a neural network) imitates an *expert* (a Monte Carlo tree search, or MCTS, that uses the apprentice to guide it). Monte Carlo means the search judges each move by averaging the results of many simulated continuations instead of solving the game exactly. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero (Silver et al., 2017) run the same loop, starting from random weights and knowing only the game rules.

blocks.title: Expert iteration as AlphaZero runs it

scenes.caption: The apprentice is one neural network. For a position s it outputs move probabilities p (an instant guess) and a value v (expected outcome). It starts from random weights.
The expert is a tree search that calls the network many times (800 simulations per move in AlphaZero). Looking ahead makes it stronger than the network alone, but far slower.
Both players pick moves with the search. At the end the game rules score the result: z is +1, 0 or -1. This outcome is the only ground truth in the loop.
Every position becomes a training example with two targets: the search's move distribution and the final outcome z.
Training pulls p toward the search policy and v toward z. The better network makes the next search stronger, which produces better targets: the loop closes.

blocks.caption: AlphaZero's loss for one position. (p, v) are the network's outputs, pi is the search's move distribution (visit counts), z the game outcome, c the weight-decay strength.

blocks.md: The cross-entropy term, $-\pi^{\top}\log \mathbf{p}$, is minus the sum over moves of $\pi_a \log p_a$. It is smallest when $\mathbf{p}$ equals $\pi$, so it pulls the network's instant guess $\mathbf{p}$ toward $\pi$, the distribution of moves the search actually explored. The squared term pulls the value $v$ toward the real outcome $z$. The last term is weight decay: it adds the squared size of all the weights $\theta$, so training prefers small weights, a standard guard against overfitting. Why is $\pi$ better than $\mathbf{p}$? Because the search combines the **prior** (the network's move probabilities $\mathbf{p}$ before any search, written $P$ below) with look-ahead: it spends simulations on moves, measures how good they turn out, and shifts visits toward the ones that score well. One **simulation** is one trip from the current position down the search tree to a position not yet evaluated; the network scores that position, and its value is credited to every move on the path.

To see that shift with numbers, take one position with 4 legal moves. The network's prior is $P = (0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05)$ for moves a, b, c, d. In this simplified toy each move leads to a position whose value is fixed: 0.45, 0.70, 0.40, 0.30 (a real search expands a deep tree and gets values from the value head, the part of the network that outputs $v$; the part that outputs $p$ is the policy head; lesson 2 runs that full search).

Each simulation picks the move with the highest score under the **pUCT** rule used by the AlphaZero family. The name stands for predictor plus UCT, Upper Confidence bounds applied to Trees. Classic UCT (Kocsis and Szepesvari, 2006) scores each move by its average value plus an optimism bonus that shrinks as the move is tried more; the predictor version scales that bonus by the network's prior. In words: the score is the measured value $Q(a)$, plus $P(a)$ times the square root of all visits so far, divided by 1 plus this move's own visits, times a factor that grows very slowly. A move the network likes but has rarely tried gets a large bonus, and every visit to it shrinks the bonus. The constants come from MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2020), DeepMind's successor to AlphaZero that also learns its own model of the game rules, so the rule is written here in MuZero's form:

blocks.tex: a^{*} = \arg\max_a \Big[ Q(a) + P(a)\,\frac{\sqrt{\sum_b N(b)}}{1 + N(a)} \Big( c_1 + \log \frac{\sum_b N(b) + c_2 + 1}{c_2} \Big) \Big]
blocks.caption: N(a) counts visits, Q(a) is the mean value seen (0 while unvisited). With c1 = 1.25 and c2 = 19652, the log term stays below 0.04 for 800 simulations, so the bonus is about 1.25 P(a) sqrt(total) / (1 + N(a)).

blocks.prompt: The prior favors move a (0.50) but move b is actually better (0.70 versus 0.45). After 800 simulations, roughly what share of the visits goes to b?
blocks.reveal: **711 of 800, or 0.889.** Move a gets only 68 (0.085). The prior decides where the first simulations go, but the bonus term decays like $1/(1+N)$ while $Q$ is a measured average, so after a few dozen visits the values dominate. The script that runs this rule exactly gives visits 68, 711, 17, 4.

blocks.title: Prior versus search visits at one position (toy)

scenes.caption: The network's prior p: it likes move a (0.50). Simplified toy: each move's result has a fixed value (a 0.45, b 0.70, c 0.40, d 0.30) instead of a deep search tree.
After 10 simulations: visits 4, 6, 0, 0. The prior sent the first simulation to a, but b's higher value already wins most visits.
After 50 simulations: 13, 34, 3, 0. The exploration bonus shrinks like 1/(1+N), so the measured value Q matters more with every visit.
After 200 simulations: 31, 160, 7, 2.
After 800 simulations: 68, 711, 17, 4. The visit distribution, 0.085 / 0.889 / 0.021 / 0.005, is the training target for p. It is a better policy than the prior.

Round 2, assuming training fits the target exactly: the new prior is the old visit share, and a fresh 800-simulation search gives 10, 788, 2, 0. Simplified: the toy keeps move values fixed; in real training the value head is retrained too.
Round 3: 0, 800, 0, 0. The policy has sharpened onto b. Move d now has prior 0 and gets no visits at all, so if its value estimate were wrong the loop could never discover it.

blocks.md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

The last two scenes show the double edge. If the values are right, iterating sharpens the policy onto the best move. If an estimate is wrong, the loop can lock in the mistake, because a move with prior 0 gets no exploration bonus. AlphaZero counters this by adding **Dirichlet noise** to the root prior, the prior at the position where each search starts. A Dirichlet distribution produces random probability vectors. AlphaZero draws one, $\eta$, and searches with $0.75\,P + 0.25\,\eta$, so every legal move keeps some prior and therefore some exploration bonus. Its parameter $\alpha$ sets how spiky the noise is: a small $\alpha$ puts most of the noise on a few random moves. AlphaZero scaled $\alpha$ inversely to the typical number of legal moves, giving 0.3, 0.15 and 0.03 for chess, shogi and Go. It also samples training moves in proportion to visit counts instead of always playing the most visited move, so lower-ranked moves still get played and scored.

AlphaGo Zero also *gated* each new network: it replaced the best player only if it won by a 55% margin. AlphaZero dropped the gate and keeps updating one network. Trained for 700,000 steps, each on a batch of 4,096 positions, it passed Stockfish, the 2016 world computer chess champion built on hand-tuned evaluation rules, in chess after about 4 hours (300,000 steps).

A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

blocks.question: Why does training the policy head on MCTS visit counts improve the network instead of just copying it?
options: Visit counts are smoother than the prior, so the cross-entropy loss is lower
The search samples at a higher temperature, so the targets are more diverse
The search mixes the prior with measured look-ahead values, so the visit counts differ from the prior where look-ahead finds better moves
The visit counts include moves from human expert games
blocks.explain: The search is an improvement operator: it starts from the prior and moves visits toward moves whose measured values are higher. In the toy, the prior said 0.30 for b and the search said 0.889. Imitating that difference is the improvement. AlphaZero uses no human games.

blocks.question: After three rounds in the toy, move d has prior 0. Suppose d was actually the best move and its value estimate was wrong. What happens in later rounds without exploration noise?
options: d is never visited, because its exploration bonus is P(d) times something, which is 0, and its Q stays 0
800 simulations are enough that the search reaches d eventually
The value loss on z will raise P(d) automatically
The gate at 55% will reject the network and restore d
blocks.explain: The pUCT bonus is proportional to the prior. With P(d) = 0 and an unvisited Q of 0, d never has the highest score, so the search never looks at it and the outcome z never reflects it. This is exactly why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior during self-play.

lessons.title: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup

blocks.md: Lesson 1's toy searched one level with fixed values. A real AlphaZero search grows a tree several moves deep, asks the network about each new position, and passes what it learns back up to the root. To watch every number, take the smallest game with real depth, **Nim with 5 stones**: players alternate taking 1 or 2 stones, and whoever takes the last stone wins. You move first. The right move is take 2: it leaves 3, and whatever the opponent takes, you take the rest. A pile that is a multiple of 3 is lost for the player to move.

The tree stores positions as **nodes** and moves as **edges**. In AlphaGo Zero each edge keeps four numbers: the visit count $N$, the total value $W$ of all evaluations passed through it, the mean value $Q = W/N$, and the prior $P$ from the policy head. Classic MCTS finishes each simulation with a random playout to the end of the game and selects moves by value and visit counts alone. AlphaGo Zero changes two things: there are no random playouts to the end of the game, because the value head scores the new position instead, and selection uses the prior through pUCT.

Our toy network, by pile size, for the player to move:

- Priors: at 5 stones take 1 gets 0.6 and take 2 gets 0.4 (it prefers the losing move); at 4 and 3, 0.5 each; at 2, take 1 gets 0.4 and take 2 gets 0.6; at 1 only take 1 is legal.
- Values: 5 stones +0.2, 4 stones +0.1, 3 stones -0.1, 2 stones +0.4, 1 stone +0.6. They all have the right sign (5, 4, 2 and 1 stones are wins for the player to move, 3 is a loss), but all are far from the true +1 or -1.

A position with 0 stones is a finished game: the player to move has lost, so its value is exactly -1 and no network is needed.

One **simulation** runs four phases, following AlphaGo Zero's Methods section (which merges expansion and evaluation into one step):

1. **Selection**: from the root, while the current node has children, move to the child with the highest $Q + U$, where $U = c\,P\sqrt{\sum_b N_b}/(1+N)$ is the pUCT bonus (here $c = 1.25$; lesson 1's MuZero form is the same at these small counts). At a node whose children are all unvisited every score is 0; we break the tie by the higher prior, an implementation choice.
2. **Expansion**: the leaf gets one child per legal move, with priors from the policy head.
3. **Evaluation**: the value head gives $v$ for the player to move at the leaf (or the exact -1 at a finished game).
4. **Backup**: walk back to the root, adding 1 to $N$ and the value to $W$ on every edge of the path.

blocks.tex: N(s_k,a_k) \mathrel{+}= 1, \qquad W(s_k,a_k) \mathrel{+}= (-1)^{L-k}\, v, \qquad Q(s_k,a_k) = \frac{W(s_k,a_k)}{N(s_k,a_k)}, \quad k = L-1, \dots, 0
blocks.caption: The path is s_0 (root), a_0, s_1, ..., s_L (leaf). v is for the player to move at s_L, so the last move (made by the other player) gets -v, the move before it +v, and so on: the sign flips at every ply.

blocks.md: The sign flip is the two-player part. Each $Q$ is stored from the point of view of the player who chose that edge, so at every node the selection rule simply maximizes, whoever is to move. AlphaGo Zero's value $v$ estimates the probability that the current player wins, and MuZero's published pseudocode makes the flip explicit: a node adds the value if its player matches the leaf's player, and its negative otherwise.

blocks.title: Twelve simulations of AlphaZero-style MCTS on 5-stone Nim

scenes.caption: Simulation 1: the root has no children yet, so it is the leaf. Expand it (priors 0.6 for take 1, 0.4 for take 2) and evaluate it: v = 0.2. Badges show visits N and mean value Q for the player who moved into a node.
Simulation 2: no child is visited, so every bonus is 0 and the tie goes to the higher prior, take 1. The value head says 4 stones is worth +0.1 for the opponent, so your Q for take 1 is -0.10.
Simulation 3: take 1 scores -0.10 + 1.25 x 0.6 x 1/2 = 0.275, take 2 scores 0 + 1.25 x 0.4 x 1/1 = 0.5. Take 2 wins; 3 stones is worth -0.1 to the opponent, so your Q for take 2 is +0.10.

Simulation 4 goes one ply deeper and expands 2 stones, where you are to move: v = +0.4 for you. Backup flips the sign each ply: the opponent's edge gets -0.4, yours gets +0.4, so Q for take 2 is (0.1 + 0.4) / 2 = 0.25.

Simulations 5 and 6: one visit deepens take 1 (3 stones under it, worth -0.1 to you, so +0.1 for the opponent's move), one reaches 1 stone (v = +0.6 for you). Q for take 2 is now (0.1 + 0.4 + 0.6) / 3 = 0.367.

Simulation 7 reaches a finished game: you took the last stone. No network call: the rules give -1 to the player to move (the opponent), so +1 is backed up for your move, -1 for theirs, +1 at the root edge.

After 12 simulations: take 2 has 9 visits and Q +0.79, take 1 has 2 and Q -0.10. Under take 2 both opponent replies now look lost (Q -0.85, -0.90), which the value head (-0.1 at 3 stones) barely knew.

blocks.prompt: Just after simulation 3, take 1 has N = 1, Q = -0.10 and take 2 has N = 1, Q = +0.10, so the root's children hold 2 visits in total. Which root move does simulation 4 select, and why?
blocks.reveal: **Take 2.** Its score is $0.10 + 1.25 \times 0.4 \times \sqrt{2}/2 = 0.454$; take 1 scores $-0.10 + 1.25 \times 0.6 \times \sqrt{2}/2 = 0.430$. The prior still favors take 1, but take 2's measured value now outweighs the difference. From here the gap widens: each backup from below take 2 brings values of +0.4, +0.6 and then +1.

blocks.code:
import math
PRIOR = {5: {1: .6, 2: .4}, 4: {1: .5, 2: .5}, 3: {1: .5, 2: .5},
         2: {1: .4, 2: .6}, 1: {1: 1.0}}           # toy policy head
VALUE = {5: .2, 4: .1, 3: -.1, 2: .4, 1: .6}       # toy value head, player to move

class Node:
    def __init__(s, pile, prior):
        s.pile, s.P, s.N, s.W, s.kids = pile, prior, 0, 0.0, {}
    def Q(s):                     # mean value for the player who moved INTO s
        return s.W / s.N if s.N else 0.0

def pick(node, c=1.25):           # pUCT; ties go to the higher prior
    tot = sum(k.N for k in node.kids.values())
    return max(node.kids.values(),
               key=lambda k: (k.Q() + c * k.P * math.sqrt(tot) / (1 + k.N), k.P))

def simulate(root):
    path = [root]
    while path[-1].kids:          # 1. selection
        path.append(pick(path[-1]))
    leaf = path[-1]
    if leaf.pile == 0:            # game over: the player to move has lost
        v = -1.0
    else:                         # 2. expansion, 3. evaluation by the value head
        leaf.kids = {a: Node(leaf.pile - a, p) for a, p in PRIOR[leaf.pile].items()}
        v = VALUE[leaf.pile]
    for n in reversed(path):      # 4. backup, sign flips every ply
        n.N += 1
        n.W -= v                  # credit the player who moved into n
        v = -v

root = Node(5, 1.0)
for _ in range(12):
    simulate(root)
for a, k in root.kids.items():
    print(f"take {a}: N={k.N} Q={k.Q():+.3f} pi(tau=1)={k.N / (root.N - 1):.3f}")

The whole search in about 40 lines (Python, standard library only). Real output:
take 1: N=2 Q=-0.100 pi(tau=1)=0.182
take 2: N=9 Q=+0.789 pi(tau=1)=0.818
The first simulation expands the root itself, so the children hold 11 of the 12 visits.

blocks.md: The search turned a prior of (0.6, 0.4) into visit counts (2, 9). That is the policy target $\pi$ from lesson 1. Why train on visits and not on $Q$? A move's $Q$ is an average over however many evaluations reached it: take 1's -0.10 rests on two shallow guesses from the value head. Visits combine prior and value and pile up only where the search kept confirming a move, so they measure how much the search trusts it. The AlphaGo Zero paper reports that these search probabilities usually select much stronger moves than the network's raw policy, which is why imitating them improves the network.

Turning visits into a move uses a **temperature** $\tau$: $\pi(a) \propto N(a)^{1/\tau}$. With $\tau = 1$, moves are played in proportion to visits; as $\tau \to 0$, the most visited move is always played. In AlphaGo Zero's self-play the first 30 moves of each game use $\tau = 1$, so the games reach a diverse set of positions, and the rest use $\tau \to 0$; evaluation games always pick the most visited move. MuZero's pseudocode for board games uses the same 30-move switch. The policy target stays the visit distribution at the root.

blocks.title: From prior to move choice at the 5-stone root

scenes.caption: The network's prior: 0.6 on take 1, the losing move.
Visit shares after 12 simulations, tau = 1: 2/11 = 0.182 and 9/11 = 0.818. This is the training target and, early in a game, the move distribution.
tau = 0.5 squares the counts before normalizing: 4/85 = 0.047 and 81/85 = 0.953.
tau near 0, used after move 30 and in evaluation games: always the most visited move.

blocks.md: Search work is not thrown away between moves. After you play take 2, the node for 3 stones becomes the new root, and AlphaGo Zero keeps its subtree with all its statistics (here 9 visits, and both opponent replies already explored) while the rest of the tree is discarded. The next search starts from that knowledge instead of from zero. Simplified: the real search also adds Dirichlet noise at the root (lesson 1), runs 800 or 1,600 simulations in parallel threads, and AlphaGo Zero evaluates leaves under a random board rotation or reflection.

Backup is where look-ahead becomes knowledge: exact outcomes and value estimates deep in the tree are averaged into the root's $Q$ values, with the sign flipped at every ply so each player maximizes their own result. The visit counts that result are the improved policy the network imitates.

A common bug: backing up $v$ with the same sign at every level. Then the edge into a leaf is credited with the value for the player who did not choose it, and each player's search prefers moves that are good for the opponent. Store each $Q$ from the point of view of the player who made the move, and flip the sign once per ply.

blocks.question: In a two-player search, the backup adds +v to every edge on the path, where v is the value for the player to move at the leaf. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; Q is symmetric between players
The search spends too many visits on the prior
Every second level is credited from the wrong player's view, so selection there favors moves that help the opponent
Visit counts stop growing
blocks.explain: The player to move at the leaf did not choose the last edge; the opponent did. Crediting that edge with +v rewards the opponent's move for being good for you. Flipping the sign at each ply keeps every Q in the chooser's point of view.

blocks.question: After the 12 simulations you play take 2. What does the next search start with at its root (3 stones, opponent to move)?
options: An empty tree, because each move needs a fresh search
The retained subtree: the 3-stone node keeps its visits and both explored replies with their N and Q
Only the prior from the network, since Q values are reset after each move
The whole old tree including the take 1 branch
blocks.explain: AlphaGo Zero reuses the tree: the child for the played move becomes the new root, its subtree is kept with all statistics, and the rest of the tree is discarded. The 9 visits already spent under take 2 count toward the next decision.

lessons.title: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune

blocks.md: Language reasoning has no game tree, but it has a cheap improvement operator when answers can be checked: **sample several solutions, keep only those whose final answer is correct, and fine-tune on them**. The filtered set is better than what the model produces on average, so imitating it is an improvement, exactly like imitating the search in lesson 1.

**STaR**, the Self-Taught Reasoner (Zelikman et al., 2022), was the first version for chain-of-thought, where the model writes out its reasoning steps before the final answer. That written reasoning is called a **rationale**. STaR used GPT-J (an open model from EleutherAI with 6B parameters), a few-shot prompt (a prompt that shows a handful of worked examples) with about 10 hand-written rationales, and datasets with answers but no rationales. It adds **rationalization**: for a question the model gets wrong, give it the correct answer as a hint, ask for a rationale, and keep it if it reaches that answer, as if no hint had been given. In symbols, it samples a rationale $r$ given both the question $x$ and the answer $y$, written $p(r \mid x, y)$, instead of given the question alone.

blocks.title: One STaR iteration on three questions (simplified)

scenes.caption: STaR starts from a pretrained model M and a dataset of questions with known answers but no rationales. A few-shot prompt with about 10 worked rationales makes M write a rationale before answering.
Question 1: the model's rationale ends in answer b, which matches the key. The rationale is kept.
Question 2: the model answers d, the key says a. Rationalization: show the correct answer as a hint and ask for a rationale. It reaches a, so it is kept, stored without the hint.
Question 3: wrong without the hint and still wrong with it. Nothing is kept, so this question gives no training signal this round.
Fine-tune on the kept rationales, starting again from the original M rather than from the last checkpoint, then repeat with the new model generating the data.

blocks.tex: \nabla J = \sum_i \mathbb{E}_{\hat r_i, \hat y_i \sim p_M(\cdot \mid x_i)} \big[ \mathbb{1}(\hat y_i = y_i)\, \nabla \log p_M(\hat y_i, \hat r_i \mid x_i) \big]

abla \log p_M(z \mid x)$. That is a Monte Carlo estimate of the gradient above.

blocks.md: Two caveats make STaR an approximation, as its authors say. Many gradient steps are taken on one batch of samples, and each iteration restarts fine-tuning from the original pretrained model, so the model being trained is not the one that drew the data: the data is off-policy. And STaR decodes greedily rather than sampling, which lowers variance but explores fewer rationales. Rationalization goes further off-policy: its rationales come from the hint-conditioned model $p(r \mid x, y)$, which the STaR paper frames as an off-policy estimate using a different proposal distribution.

So STaR is a crude form of the RL you know from GRPO: reward 1 for correct, 0 otherwise, but with no baseline, no negative signal from wrong answers, and many gradient steps on one batch of samples. Rationalization exists because without it the loop stalls: a question the model never solves never enters the training set. On CommonsenseQA (5-way multiple-choice questions that need everyday knowledge) the results were: few-shot chain-of-thought GPT-J 36.6%, GPT-J fine-tuned to answer directly 60.0%, STaR without rationalization 68.8%, STaR with it 72.5%, close to 73.0% for a fine-tuned GPT-3 that is 30x larger.

Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

**ReST-EM** (Singh et al., 2023) scales the idea up. Instead of one greedy sample (always taking the most likely next token, so the same answer every time), draw many random samples per problem: 32 for MATH (12,500 competition math problems) and 64 for APPS (Python programming problems that come with test cases). Sampling uses top-K 40 (only the 40 most likely tokens can be chosen at each step) and temperature 0.7 (logits are divided by 0.7 before the softmax, which sharpens the distribution). A binary reward checks the final answer (MATH) or runs test cases (APPS). Keep at most 10 correct solutions per problem, fine-tune the base model on them, and repeat. ReST-EM drops rationalization. The paper derives the loop as **expectation-maximization** (EM), a classic algorithm for fitting a model when part of the data is hidden: alternate between inferring the hidden part with the current model (the E-step) and refitting the model to that inference (the M-step). Here the hidden part is which samples are good.

blocks.tex: q_{t+1}(y \mid x) \propto r(x,y)\, p_{\theta_t}(y \mid x), \qquad \theta_{t+1} = \arg\max_\theta \ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\theta_t}} \big[ r(x,y) \log p_\theta(y \mid x) \big]
blocks.caption: ReST-EM as expectation-maximization. E-step: reweight the current model's samples by reward (with 0/1 rewards: keep the correct ones). M-step: maximize reward-weighted log-likelihood (fine-tune on them).

blocks.md: Read the formula this way: the new target $q$ is the current model's distribution multiplied by the reward, so with 0/1 rewards it is the model restricted to correct answers, and the new weights are the ones that make those answers most likely. Unlike online RL, sampling uses a model that stays fixed for the whole iteration, so data collection and training are decoupled: generate one big dataset, then train on it. The ReST-EM paper notes this makes the method easier to scale to very large models.

blocks.prompt: Five problems have per-sample success rates 0.9, 0.5, 0.1, 0.02 and 0. With one sample each, the expected number of problems that contribute a correct solution is 0.9 + 0.5 + 0.1 + 0.02 + 0 = 1.52. What is it with 32 samples each?
blocks.reveal: **3.44.** Each problem contributes with probability $1-(1-p)^{32}$: 1.000, 1.000, 0.966, 0.476 and 0. More samples mostly help the hard problems, which is where new skill comes from. The problem with $p = 0$ stays at 0: no amount of sampling helps, which is why STaR added rationalization.

blocks.title: Chance that a problem yields at least one correct sample

scenes.caption: With one sample per problem, a problem the model solves 10% of the time contributes a training example only 10% of the time.
With N = 8 the same problem yields a correct solution with probability 0.570.
N = 32, as ReST-EM uses on MATH: 0.966 for p = 0.1 and 0.476 for p = 0.02. More samples reach further into the hard tail.
N = 64, as ReST-EM uses on APPS: 0.726 for p = 0.02. But at p = 0 the curve is 0 for every N: sampling cannot find what the model never produces.

blocks.title: Sample, check, cap: one seeded draw of 8 samples

scenes.caption: Five training problems, 8 samples each (shown small; ReST-EM draws 32 or 64). Each sample is a full solution whose final answer will be checked.
The checker marks each sample. This seeded draw got 7, 4, 1, 0 and 0 correct. P4 is solvable in principle (p = 0.02) but was unlucky; P5 never will be.
Cap at 3 correct per problem (ReST-EM caps at 10). P1's extra 4 correct samples are dropped, so the easy problem no longer dominates the fine-tuning set.

blocks.md: Why cap at 10? With 32 samples the expected number of correct solutions is 28.8, 16, 3.2, 0.64 and 0 for our five problems, so the easiest problem would be 59% of the fine-tuning data. With the cap, the expected kept counts are 10, 9.99, 3.2, 0.64 and 0, and the shares become 42%, 42%, 13% and 3%. The two hard problems double their weight.

Results: on PaLM 2 models (Google's 2023 language models, in a small and a large size), fine-tuning on ReST-EM's self-generated solutions beat fine-tuning on human-written solutions for MATH and APPS, and the gain was larger for the bigger model. But most of the improvement came in the first iteration. Training accuracy kept rising with more iterations while test accuracy flattened on MATH and dropped on APPS in iteration 2, which the authors attribute to overfitting a small set of training problems (7,500 for MATH, 2,342 for APPS).

blocks.question: Your ReST-EM run uses 64 samples per problem, yet 20% of training problems never get a correct sample. Which change gives the model a training signal on exactly those problems?
options: Train for more epochs on the solutions you already kept
Lower the sampling temperature so solutions are more careful
Continue fine-tuning from the last checkpoint instead of the base model
STaR's rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and keep rationales that reach it
blocks.explain: Problems with no correct sample are invisible to the filter; more training on kept data or lower temperature cannot add them. Rationalization samples from a different distribution, p(r | x, y), which can reach the answer. The cost, covered in lesson 5, is more rationales that reach the right answer for the wrong reasons.

blocks.question: Why does ReST-EM cap the number of correct solutions kept per problem?
options: Easy problems produce many more correct samples, so without a cap they would dominate the fine-tuning set
Storage: 64 solutions per problem would not fit in memory
The verifier becomes unreliable after 10 solutions
To keep the dataset exactly the same size every iteration
blocks.explain: With 32 samples, a problem solved 90% of the time contributes about 28.8 solutions and one solved 10% of the time about 3.2. The cap of 10 rebalances the data toward harder problems; the paper says it keeps diversity and prevents overfitting to easy problems.

lessons.title: Build a STaR loop: sample, filter, fine-tune, repeat

blocks.md: Lessons 3 and 5 made claims you can check on a laptop: the first iteration gives most of the gain, held-out accuracy can fall while training accuracy rises, and rationalization lets in reasoning that is wrong but ends at the right answer. This lab runs a STaR loop (with ReST-EM-style sampling and a cap) small enough to finish in 20 to 30 minutes per run and measures each one. The tiny example to keep in mind: one question, 8 sampled rationales, 2 of them correct, both kept and fine-tuned on.

Setup. The model is Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (0.5 billion parameters, Alibaba's Qwen family). The task is a synthetic three-step word problem: multiply a three-digit by a two-digit number, subtract, then divide exactly. Because we generate the problems, we know the answer and also the intermediate numbers, so we can check the *reasoning*, not just the answer. 192 training questions, 200 held-out questions. Per iteration: sample $N = 8$ rationales per training question at temperature 0.7, keep up to 3 correct ones, fine-tune a fresh LoRA adapter (low-rank weight updates, rank 16 on the attention projections) on the *base* model for 2 epochs, repeat 3 times.

blocks.caption: The task generator, the prompt and the checker. The checker reads 'Answer: N', else the last boxed number, else the last integer: the base model often ignores the format, so a strict checker would mostly measure formatting. mid holds the product and the remainder, used later to audit reasoning.

blocks.code:
def star_iteration(tok, model):
    """Sample N rationales per question, keep correct ones (cap), rationalize the rest."""
    outs = generate(tok, model, [prompt_text(tok, p["q"]) for p in train], n=N, temperature=T)
    keep, n_ok, unsolved = [], 0, []
    for p, samples in zip(train, outs):
        ok = [s for s in samples if extract(s) == p["a"]]
        n_ok += len(ok)
        keep += [(p["q"], s) for s in ok[:CAP]]
        if not ok:
            unsolved.append(p)
    n_rat = 0
    if RAT and unsolved:
        hinted = generate(tok, model, [prompt_text(tok, p["q"], hint=p["a"]) for p in unsolved],
                          n=1, temperature=T)
        for p, (s,) in zip(unsolved, hinted):
            if extract(s) == p["a"] and "hint" not in s.lower():   # store without the hint
                keep.append((p["q"], s)); n_rat += 1
    return keep, n_ok / (N * len(train)), len(unsolved), n_rat
blocks.caption: One STaR iteration: sample, filter, cap, rationalize. Hinted rationales are stored with the plain prompt; any that mention the hint are dropped. Not shown: N, CAP, T = 8, 3, 0.7; train is 192 make_problem questions; generate wraps Hugging Face model.generate with sampling.

blocks.code:
def finetune_from_base(tok, keep, out_dir, epochs=2, lr=2e-4, bs=8):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL, dtype=torch.float32).to(DEV)
    model = get_peft_model(base, LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.0,
                                            target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"]))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW([q for q in model.parameters() if q.requires_grad], lr=lr)
    tok.padding_side = "right"
    for ep in range(epochs):
        random.Random(ep).shuffle(keep)
        for i in range(0, len(keep), bs):
            batch = keep[i:i + bs]
            prompts = [prompt_text(tok, q) for q, _ in batch]
            full = [pr + r + tok.eos_token for pr, (_, r) in zip(prompts, batch)]
            enc = tok(full, return_tensors="pt", padding=True).to(DEV)
            labels = enc["input_ids"].clone()
            for j, pr in enumerate(prompts):                     # train on rationale tokens only
                labels[j, :len(tok(pr)["input_ids"])] = -100
            labels[enc["attention_mask"] == 0] = -100
            loss = model(**enc, labels=labels).loss
            loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
    tok.padding_side = "left"
    model.save_pretrained(out_dir)
    del model, base
    torch.mps.empty_cache() if DEV == "mps" else None
blocks.caption: Fine-tune from the base model every iteration, as STaR and ReST-EM do. Labels are -100 (ignored) on prompt and padding tokens, so only rationale tokens are trained. Run on an Apple-silicon laptop GPU (MPS), float32; one iteration (1,536 samples, about 300 kept, 2 epochs) took 6 to 20 minutes.

blocks.md: We ran the loop twice from the same start: once with rationalization (questions with no correct sample get one hinted attempt) and once without. Held-out accuracy is greedy decoding on the 200 test questions; training accuracy is the share of correct samples among the 1,536 drawn that iteration. Both are single runs with one seed, so differences of a few points are noise.

blocks.title: Real runs: accuracy across STaR iterations

scenes.caption: Without rationalization, training-sample accuracy: 16.7%, 33.3%, 42.0% (no sample is drawn after the last fine-tune). It keeps rising: the model gets better at its own training questions.

Without rationalization, held-out greedy accuracy: 32.5%, 40.5%, 35.0%, 34.5%. Nearly all the gain comes in iteration 1, then it slips while training accuracy still climbs, the pattern ReST-EM reported.
With rationalization, held-out greedy accuracy: 32.5%, 32.0%, 30.5%, 22.0%. Same loop, same questions, plus 20, 17 and 43 hinted rationales per iteration, and in this single run the model got worse.

blocks.prompt: The rationalization run kept 20, 17 and 43 hinted rationales. Each one reaches the right answer. Guess what share of them show the correct product (the first intermediate number).
blocks.reveal: **Only about 1 in 10.** Of the hinted rationales, 17 of 20, 15 of 17 and 39 of 43 do *not* contain the correct product. The model writes wrong arithmetic, then jumps to the number it was told. Among ordinary kept samples the rate is 3 of 189, 13 of 271 and 20 of 285. The hint makes it easy to write any story that ends at the answer, exactly the false positives ReST-EM warned about.

blocks.md: Why worse here, in this single run, than in the STaR paper, where rationalization helped? The drop fits the audit above, though one seed cannot prove the cause. STaR used a 6B model on CommonsenseQA, where a rationale is a short argument, not arithmetic a small model gets wrong; and STaR's hint is inside few-shot examples of good rationalizations. A 0.5B model asked for a 3-digit product will happily invent one. The lesson is not that rationalization is bad, but that you must audit what it lets in: here a check of the intermediate number would have rejected almost all of it.

A second check uses the held-out questions with 4 samples each at temperature 0.7, in the rationalization run. Sampled accuracy went 21.6%, 27.8%, 27.5%, 23.5%, while pass@4 (at least one of 4 correct) barely moved: 42.5%, 44.5%, 44.0%, 41.5%. Iteration 1 mostly made the model's samples more like its best answer rather than teaching it to solve new questions, and the share of questions it can solve at all stayed flat. Answers also got shorter: 96.6 words on average at the start, 78.2 after iteration 3.

Last, the filter itself. Lesson 5's formula says a final-answer check lets in more lucky rationales when a wrong attempt can still land on the key. We asked the base model the same 96 training questions two ways, 8 samples each: with a numeric answer, and as 4-way multiple choice (the right answer plus three nearby wrong numbers). A kept rationale is called flawed if its text is missing the correct product or the correct final value.

blocks.title: Flawed share of kept rationales, base model (real run)

scenes.caption: Numeric answers: 1 flawed of 123 kept (0.8%). A wrong calculation almost never lands on the exact integer.

Multiple choice: 22 flawed of 122 kept (18.0%), from the same model on the same questions. The formula with the measured rates (sound reasoning q = 0.164, a flawed attempt picks the right letter c = 0.034) predicts 14.9%.

blocks.md: The measured $c$ is 0.034, far below the 0.25 of uniform guessing: a flawed calculation usually points at no option or a wrong one, and the model often fails to output a letter. The formula is still in the right range (14.9% against 18.0%); the gap comes partly from 26 samples with sound working that still picked the wrong letter, which the formula assumes away. The direction is the lesson: the same model, the same questions, and a smaller answer space let in more than 20 times as many flawed rationales.

Measure the filter, not just the score. Two cheap audits caught what accuracy alone hid: check an intermediate quantity on a sample of kept data, and track held-out accuracy every iteration, since training accuracy rises regardless.

To scale this up, swap in GSM8K with its 7,473 training questions, sample with a fast inference engine, and keep the same audit columns: kept count, unsolved count, flawed share, train and held-out accuracy per iteration. Simplified here: one seed, a synthetic task, and a lenient answer extractor.

blocks.question: In the run without rationalization, training-sample accuracy rose from 16.7% to 42.0% while held-out greedy accuracy went 32.5%, 40.5%, 35.0%, 34.5%. What is the best reading?
options: The held-out set is harder, so the numbers cannot be compared
Iteration 1 helped; later iterations fit the same 192 training questions more closely without adding general skill
The model collapsed because it trained on its own outputs with no filter
Greedy decoding is broken after LoRA fine-tuning
blocks.explain: The filter adds information only about the 192 training questions, so later rounds mostly sharpen the model on them. ReST-EM saw the same shape: training accuracy rising, test accuracy flat or falling after the first iteration. This is not collapse, since every kept sample passed the checker.

blocks.question: Your rationalized rationales reach the hinted answer, but an audit shows 9 in 10 state a wrong intermediate product. What is the most direct fix?
options: Drop rationalization, or keep a hinted rationale only if its intermediate numbers also check out
Raise the sampling temperature for hinted attempts
Keep more hinted rationales per question
Fine-tune from the previous checkpoint instead of the base model
blocks.explain: The final-answer filter cannot see the flaw because the hint guarantees the answer. Either remove that path or strengthen the filter for it, for example by recomputing the product. STaR's own paper found that sampling at higher temperature raised the rate of right answers from wrong reasoning.

lessons.title: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting

blocks.md: In the STaR and ReST-EM loops of lessons 3 and 4 the filter is the only thing that adds information. So its errors go straight into the training set. A final-answer check accepts a solution whose reasoning is wrong but whose answer happens to match: a **false positive**. Cobbe et al., who built GSM8K (about 8,500 grade-school math word problems) and trained verifiers on it (models that read a solution and predict whether it is correct), point out exactly this: labeling solutions only by the final answer means some flawed solutions are labeled correct.

blocks.prompt: A model answers 5-way multiple-choice questions. On 30% of questions it reasons soundly and gets them right. On the rest its reasoning is flawed and its answer is effectively a random pick among the 5 options. What fraction of the rationales a STaR filter keeps are flawed?
blocks.reveal: **About 32%.** Out of 50 questions: 15 sound and correct, and 35 flawed of which $35 \times 0.2 = 7$ match the key by luck. The filter keeps $15 + 7 = 22$, and $7/22 = 0.318$. The STaR paper notes this risk directly: on CommonsenseQA a random pick is right about 20% of the time regardless of the reasoning.

blocks.title: 22 kept rationales out of 50 questions

scenes.caption: 50 five-way questions, one sample each. The filter keeps every rationale whose final answer matches the key: 22 of them. The filter cannot tell them apart.
Inside: 15 come from sound reasoning (30% of 50). The other 35 had flawed reasoning and guessed among 5 options, so about 7 landed on the key by luck. 7 of 22 is 31.8% of the training data.
Fine-tuning treats all 22 alike. The 7 lucky ones teach the model that plausible but wrong reasoning ending in the right letter is good reasoning.

blocks.caption: q is the rate of sound reasoning, c the chance a flawed attempt still lands on the right answer. Simplified: it assumes flawed attempts guess uniformly.

blocks.title: Share of kept rationales that are lucky guesses

params.name: c
params.label: chance a guess is right, c

scenes.caption: Five-way multiple choice (c = 0.2). Early in training, when q is small, lucky guesses are a large part of the kept data: 64% at q = 0.1 and 31.8% at q = 0.3.
Four options (c = 0.25): worse at every q, for example 36.8% at q = 0.3.
A numeric answer that is hard to guess (c = 0.01): 2.3% at q = 0.3. A large answer space makes the same filter far more precise. Simplified: real flawed reasoning is not a uniform guess.

blocks.md: Two experimental findings fit this picture. STaR tried a natural alternative to rationalization, sampling more at higher temperature, and found it counterproductive: it raised the chance of a correct answer from wrong reasoning, and training on that reasoning hurt generalization. ReST-EM reports that in preliminary experiments rationalization substantially increased false positives, correct answers with incorrect reasoning, which is one reason it uses plain sampling instead. Giving the model the answer makes it easier to write any story that ends there.

Prefer checks with a large answer space and several independent conditions. A numeric answer or a program that must pass a set of unit tests is rarely right by luck; a single multiple-choice letter often is. When a checker is weak, also inspect samples of the kept data by hand.

The second failure mode appears when the filter is a learned **reward model** instead of an exact check. ReST (Gulcehre et al., 2023), the predecessor of ReST-EM, trained machine translation with a learned quality metric as reward. It alternates a *Grow* step (sample a dataset from the policy) with several *Improve* steps that fine-tune on samples above a threshold $\tau$, raising $\tau$ each time. Reward model scores kept rising with more Grow steps, but human raters preferred the model after **one** Grow step. The authors warn that the risk of overfitting to the reward model grows with repeated Grow steps.

The third failure mode is plain overfitting. A verifier only adds information about the problems you have. In ReST-EM, training accuracy rose steadily across iterations while test accuracy stalled on MATH and fell on APPS in iteration 2. Compare model collapse from the prerequisite course: there the loop added no information at all. Here it adds some each round, but always about the same finite set of problems.

A self-improvement loop is only as good as its filter. The precision of the check sets the quality of the kept data, and the set of problems the model can sometimes solve sets how far the loop can reach.

blocks.question: For which task would a STaR-style final-answer filter keep the fewest flawed rationales, for the same model accuracy?
options: True or false questions
5-way multiple choice questions
Competition math problems with an integer answer
Open-ended summaries scored by a learned reward model
blocks.explain: The flawed share depends on c, the chance a flawed attempt matches anyway. It is 0.5 for true or false, 0.2 for 5 options, and tiny for an integer answer. A learned reward model adds its own errors on top, as ReST's human evaluation showed.

blocks.question: In ReST, reward model scores keep rising with every Grow step, but human raters prefer the model after one Grow step. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The policy is increasingly exploiting errors in the learned reward model, a proxy for human judgment
Human raters are noisier than the reward model, so their results should be ignored
The Improve thresholds were set too low
Translation quality cannot improve after one Grow step for any method
blocks.explain: The reward model is only a proxy. Optimizing a proxy harder eventually finds outputs it overrates. The ReST authors say exactly this and suggest periodically refreshing the reward model with human labels on the newest policy's outputs.

lessons.title: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs

blocks.md: Lessons 3 to 5 needed answers you can check. For open-ended chat there is no answer key. Two methods replace it with something already at hand. **SPIN** uses the existing human SFT data as the target. **Self-Rewarding LMs** use the model itself as the judge.

**SPIN**, Self-Play fIne-tuNing (Chen et al., 2024), starts from a supervised fine-tuned model. For each prompt $x$ in the SFT data, the previous iteration's model generates a response $y'$. The new model is trained to tell the human response $y$ apart from $y'$. The paper frames this as a game between two copies of one LLM: the *main player* (new model) learns to distinguish, the *opponent* (old model) tries to produce responses that cannot be distinguished. Next iteration, the new model becomes the opponent.

blocks.caption: y is the human response, y' is a sample from the previous model p_theta_t, lambda, a positive number, controls how far one iteration moves.

blocks.md: Read the loss this way. Each log ratio measures how much more likely the new model makes a response than the old model $p_{\theta_t}$ did. The loss takes the ratio for the human response $y$, subtracts the ratio for the model's own sample $y'$, scales the difference by $\lambda$, and applies the logistic loss $\ell(t) = \log(1 + e^{-t})$, which is near 0 when $t$ is large and positive and grows when $t$ is negative. So training raises the human response and lowers the old model's own habits.

This is the shape of the **DPO** loss. Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) fine-tunes on preference pairs (a prompt, a chosen response and a rejected one) without training a reward model, using exactly this loss with log ratios taken against a frozen reference model (usually the SFT model) and a strength $\beta$ in the place of $\lambda$. SPIN is that loss with three substitutions: the reference model is the previous iteration, the *chosen* response is always the human one, and the *rejected* response is always the model's own sample. No preference labels or reward model are needed. In an idealized setting where the model can be any distribution, the paper proves that once $p_{\theta_t} = p_{\text{data}}$ the current model already minimizes the loss, so training stops there, and derives how one iteration moves the opponent:

blocks.tex: p_{t+1}(y \mid x) \ \propto\ p_t(y \mid x) \left( \frac{p_{\text{data}}(y \mid x)}{p_t(y \mid x)} \right)^{1/\lambda}
blocks.caption: Each probability is multiplied by (p_data / p_t) to the power 1/lambda, then renormalized. Responses the model under-produces relative to the data gain probability; over-produced ones lose it. Smaller lambda moves faster; lambda = 1 jumps straight to p_data in this idealized form.

blocks.md: Where the update comes from, in two steps (Chen et al., Lemma C.2 and Theorem 5.4). First, forget that the main player must be an LLM and ask which scoring function $f(x, y)$ best separates human responses from the old model's under the logistic loss. The answer is $f^{*}(x, y) = \log \frac{p_{\text{data}}(y \mid x)}{p_t(y \mid x)} + Z(x)$: score each response by how much more often the data produces it than the old model does ($Z(x)$ is any per-prompt constant). Second, SPIN's main player is not free; it is $f = \lambda \log \frac{p_\theta(y \mid x)}{p_t(y \mid x)}$, the log ratio from the loss. If the best $f^{*}$ is reachable, setting the two equal gives $\lambda \log \frac{p_{t+1}}{p_t} = \log \frac{p_{\text{data}}}{p_t} + Z$, and solving for $p_{t+1}$ gives the update above, with $e^{Z/\lambda}$ as the normalizer.

The fixed point follows directly. If $p_t = p_{\text{data}}$, then $f^{*} = Z(x)$ gives every response the same score, so no function separates the two sets better than chance, and the loss gradient vanishes. The paper also proves a converse (Theorem 5.2): if $p_t \neq p_{\text{data}}$, then for a suitably chosen $\lambda$ the current model is not the minimizer, so training keeps moving.

blocks.title: SPIN's ideal update pulls the model toward the data (lambda = 2)

scenes.caption: Simplified: a prompt with only 4 possible responses. The human SFT data has p_data = 0.50, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05.
The SFT model p_0 is off: 0.20, 0.20, 0.30, 0.30. Total variation distance from the data (half the sum of absolute differences): 0.40.
Iteration 1 multiplies each probability by (p_data / p_0)^(1/2) and renormalizes: 0.353, 0.273, 0.237, 0.137. Distance 0.174.
Iteration 3: 0.466, 0.298, 0.171, 0.065. Distance 0.036, roughly halving each time.
Iteration 4: 0.483, 0.299, 0.160, 0.057. Distance 0.018. Each step changes less, because the ratio p_data / p_t approaches 1, the same shrinking gains the SPIN paper observed.

blocks.md: SPIN's fixed point is the human data distribution. It can extract more from an SFT dataset than plain SFT does, but it cannot surpass that data: once the model's responses are indistinguishable from the human ones, the loss gives no signal.

blocks.prompt: In the 4-response toy, suppose response 4 (p_data = 0.05) is factually wrong, an error in the human SFT data, and the SFT model rarely says it: p_0 = (0.40, 0.30, 0.29, 0.01). What does SPIN's ideal update (lambda = 2) do to response 4 over four iterations?
blocks.reveal: **It raises it toward 0.05: 0.023, 0.034, 0.041, 0.045.** SPIN has no notion of correct, only of *like the data*. Every response the model under-produces relative to $p_{\text{data}}$ is pushed up, errors included. The SFT data is the judge, so its mistakes become the target.

blocks.md: Experiments: SPIN fine-tuned zephyr-7b-sft-full (a Mistral-7B SFT model) using 50k prompts sampled from UltraChat200k (a cleaned set of about 200,000 multi-turn chat dialogues), training 2 epochs per iteration. The average score on the HuggingFace Open LLM Leaderboard tasks (a public ranking that averages accuracy over six standard benchmarks of knowledge, reasoning and math) rose from 58.14 to 63.16. MT-Bench (80 multi-turn questions whose answers GPT-4 grades from 1 to 10) rose from 5.94 to 6.78, with each iteration adding less than the one before. Continued plain SFT on the same data had plateaued or got worse.

**Self-Rewarding Language Models** (Yuan et al., 2024) go further: the model writes the preferences too. Starting from Llama 2 70B fine-tuned on 3,200 human instruction examples plus 1,630 examples of judging responses (both from Open Assistant, a crowd-sourced collection of human-written conversations with quality ratings), each iteration runs the loop below. The judge prompt adds one point per criterion met: relevance, partial coverage, a useful answer, a clear and well-organized assistant response, and expert, tailored quality. New prompts are made in the Self-Instruct style (Wang et al., 2022): show a model a few existing prompts and ask it to write a new one.

blocks.title: One Self-Rewarding iteration

scenes.caption: New prompts come from few-shot prompting in the Self-Instruct style. In the main experiments a fixed model (Llama 2-Chat 70B) writes them; an appendix shows the trained model can do it too.
The current model samples N = 4 candidate responses at temperature 0.7.
The same weights, prompted as a judge, score each response out of 5 with an additive rubric, 3 times with sampling, and average the scores.
Highest and lowest scored responses form a preference pair. If they tie, the prompt is discarded.
DPO on these pairs (beta 0.1) produces M(t+1), which is a better responder and a better judge for the next round.

blocks.md: A worked pair: four responses to one prompt receive judge samples (4, 3, 4), (5, 4, 5), (2, 3, 3) and (4, 5, 4). The averages are 3.67, 4.67, 2.67 and 4.33. The pair is response 2 (chosen) versus response 3 (rejected). If all four had averaged the same, the prompt would yield no pair. Iteration 1 produced 3,964 pairs to train M2, iteration 2 produced 6,942 pairs to train M3. The main benchmark is AlpacaEval 2.0: 805 instructions, where a GPT-4 Turbo judge compares each response with GPT-4 Turbo's own, and the win rate is the share of comparisons the model wins.

blocks.title: Self-Rewarding Llama 2 70B across iterations

scenes.caption: AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4 Turbo, judged by GPT-4 Turbo: 9.94%, 15.38%, 20.44%.
As a judge, agreement with human rankings on held-out pairs: 78.7%, 80.4%, 81.7% (an SFT model trained without judge data scored 65.1%). Policy and judge improve together.

blocks.md: Rising numbers are not proof that quality rose. Average response length on AlpacaEval grew from 1092 (M1) to 1552 (M2) to 2552 (M3), and length is known to correlate with judged quality. The authors list reward hacking (the policy scoring higher by exploiting the judge's blind spots rather than by getting better) within the framework as an open question, and note that LLMs supply both the training reward and (through GPT-4) the evaluation, which needs deeper analysis.

blocks.question: In SPIN's idealized update, set lambda = 1. What happens after one iteration?
options: The model moves halfway toward the data distribution
The model becomes exactly p_data, and further iterations change nothing
The model overshoots p_data and oscillates
Nothing, because lambda = 1 cancels the loss
blocks.explain: With 1/lambda = 1 the update is p_t times p_data / p_t, which is p_data after renormalizing. Then the ratio is 1 everywhere and the update is the identity. Real training cannot represent the ideal update exactly, which is one reason SPIN needs several iterations.

blocks.question: Why can Self-Rewarding training, at least in principle, raise its own ceiling, while SPIN cannot exceed its SFT data?
options: Self-Rewarding uses DPO and SPIN does not
Self-Rewarding trains on more prompts
In Self-Rewarding the judge is the model being trained, so its preferences can improve each iteration; SPIN always treats the fixed human response as the winner
SPIN uses a smaller base model
blocks.explain: Both losses are DPO-like. The difference is the target: SPIN's chosen response is always from the fixed human data, so p_data is the fixed point. Self-Rewarding's preferences come from a judge that is retrained every iteration, which is also why it carries a risk of reward hacking that SPIN does not.

lessons.title: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding

blocks.md: Say a model samples 16 solutions to a training problem and 5 reach the right answer. STaR and ReST-EM fine-tune on the 5 and throw away the 11 failures. But those 11 say something too: they are exactly the mistakes this model tends to make. This lesson covers loops that reuse failures or improve the judge itself, and a measure, the **generation-verification gap**, that says how far any filter-and-distill loop can go.

**V-STaR** (Hosseini et al., 2024) trains two models from the same samples. Each iteration samples $k = 16$ solutions per training problem from the current generator and labels each by its final answer (math) or by running test cases (code). Correct ones go into the generator's data $D_{GEN}$; correct *and* incorrect ones go into the verifier's data $D_{VER}$. The next generator is fine-tuned from the pretrained model on $D_{GEN}$, as in STaR. The verifier is trained with DPO on pairs (a correct and an incorrect solution to the same problem, all combinations), with the SFT model as the reference. DPO was introduced in lesson 6.

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}(V) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y^+, y^-) \sim D_{VER}} \log \sigma\big(\hat r(x, y^+) - \hat r(x, y^-)\big), \qquad \hat r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{V(y \mid x)}{G_{SFT}(y \mid x)}
blocks.caption: V-STaR's verifier loss: the DPO loss with correct solutions as chosen and incorrect ones as rejected. At test time a candidate's score is its likelihood under the trained verifier, V(y | x).

blocks.title: One V-STaR iteration
