scenes.caption: The generator samples 16 solutions per training problem. The answer key or test cases label each one: the only outside information in the loop.
STaR's half: correct solutions accumulate in D_GEN, and the next generator is fine-tuned from the pretrained model on them.
The new half: every labeled solution, failures included, goes into D_VER. Pairs of a correct and an incorrect solution train the verifier with DPO.
At test time the generator samples many candidates and the verifier picks the one it scores highest. Each iteration's better generator also makes harder negatives for the verifier.

blocks.md: Results with LLaMA2 and CodeLLaMA 7B and 13B (LoRA, 3 iterations): 6 to 17 points of absolute test accuracy over prior self-improvement and verification baselines on math (GSM8K, a MATH subset) and 4 to 12 on code (MBPP, HumanEval), reported as best-of-64 for verifier methods. The 7B V-STaR beat base LLaMA2 70B (8-shot) on GSM8K. On MBPP the gains across verifier iterations were larger than across generator iterations. A DPO verifier beat a classic outcome reward model trained on the same data, and on MBPP putting the verifier inside the training loop did not add much. In their experiments best-of-k accuracy saturated for k of 16 or more.

Now the general question: when does *verify, filter, distill* improve a model at all? Song et al. (2024, *Mind the Gap*) define the **generation-verification gap** as the accuracy of the model's samples after reweighting them by a verifier's scores, minus the accuracy before. For a 0/1 filter it is simply kept-set accuracy minus raw accuracy. The kept-set accuracy formula, in terms of the verifier's true and false positive rates, is derived in the synthetic-data-model-collapse course; here it is applied with the model as its own verifier.

blocks.tex: \text{gap}(f, g) = J\big(f[w(\hat u_g)]\big) - J(f), \qquad \text{gap}_{rel} = \frac{\text{gap}}{U_{max} - J(f)}, \qquad J(f_{t+1}) - J(f_t) \ \ge\ \text{gap}(f_t, g) - \varepsilon_{update}
blocks.caption: f generates, g verifies, J is expected accuracy, f[w(u_g)] is f's distribution reweighted by g's scores. The relative gap divides by the room left (U_max is 1 for accuracy), per prompt, then averaged. The bound: one round gains at least the gap minus the error of distilling the filtered set.

blocks.prompt: A model answers correctly 30% of the time. As its own verifier it accepts 80% of its correct answers and 20% of its wrong ones. What are the gap and the relative gap?
blocks.reveal: **Gap 0.332, relative gap 0.474.** Kept accuracy is $0.3 \times 0.8 / (0.3 \times 0.8 + 0.7 \times 0.2) = 0.24/0.38 = 0.632$, so the gap is $0.632 - 0.3 = 0.332$, and relative to the 0.7 of room left it is $0.332/0.7 = 0.474$. If distillation were perfect, one round would move the model to 0.632.

blocks.title: Generation-verification gap of a 0/1 self-verifier

curves.label: p t / (p t + (1 - p) f) - p

scenes.caption: t = 0.8, f = 0.2: the gap is 0.332 at p = 0.3, peaks at p = 1/3, and shrinks toward 0 as p approaches 1. A good model has little left for its own filter to remove.
t = f = 0.6: the verifier accepts right and wrong answers equally often, so it carries no information and the gap is 0 at every p.
t = 0.9, f = 0.05: a sharper verifier gives a gap of 0.585 at p = 0.3. Self-improvement is bounded by how much better the model checks than it generates.

blocks.md: Measured on base models (sampling 128 answers per question and one self-verification each), the paper reports: small models such as Qwen-1.5 0.5B, Qwen-2 0.5B and Llama-2 7B had a gap at or below zero for nearly all verification methods; verification that writes a chain of thought before a score was more reliable than asking for the probability of a Correct label; and with such verification the *relative* gap grew steadily with pretraining compute (the authors conjecture linearly in its logarithm). Some tasks showed no gap at any size: on Natural Questions (factual recall) all gaps were under 1%, and on 4x4 Sudoku only the largest models gained.

blocks.title: Iterating with a fixed self-verifier (toy, perfect distillation)

scenes.caption: Toy: half the questions are checkable (t = 0.8, f = 0.2), half are not (t = f = 0.6). Accuracy starts at 0.3 and rises: 0.466, 0.586, 0.632, 0.645.

The gap each round: 0.166, 0.121, 0.046, 0.013, 0.003. It shrinks to about zero in a handful of rounds, the saturation Song et al. measured, because the checkable half is used up and the rest carries no signal.

blocks.md: In iterative experiments with Qwen-1.5 models from 7B to 72B on GSM8K, the gap fell close to zero within two or three rounds, at a similar rate for every size. Pass@k (the chance at least one of k samples is right) rose for small k but *fell* for large k across rounds: the model lost diversity. With a gold verifier that loss did not appear; with a stronger but imperfect verifier it still did, because on some questions the model converged on wrong answers the verifier accepted. That is the lucky false positive of lesson 5, compounded over rounds.

**Meta-Rewarding** (Wu et al., 2024) attacks the judge side of Self-Rewarding (lesson 6), which trains the model only as an actor: its judging improves only as a side effect, and the Meta-Rewarding authors hypothesize that this is why gains saturate. One model plays three roles. As **actor** it samples 7 responses per prompt. As **judge** it scores each response with the 5-point rubric 11 times and averages. As **meta-judge** it compares two of its own judgments of the same response and says which follows the rubric better, asked twice with the order swapped. For judge training it uses the response whose judge scores vary most; pairwise meta-judge wins become Elo-style scores (the chess rating method: beating a strong opponent raises a rating more than beating a weak one), and the best and worst judgments form a preference pair. Actor pairs and judge pairs are trained together with DPO.

It also adds **length control**: among responses whose scores lie within a top tier set by $\rho$, the *shortest* is the chosen one; among the bottom tier, the *longest* is rejected. Starting from Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the length-controlled AlpacaEval 2 win rate (a win rate adjusted to remove the advantage of longer answers) went from 22.92% to 39.44% after four iterations, with average length staying near 2,000 characters; Arena-Hard (harder, more complex prompts, also judged by GPT-4) went from 20.6% to 29.1%. The same pipeline without judge training (Self-Rewarding plus length control) reached 35.49%.

blocks.title: AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate (Llama-3-8B-Instruct)

scenes.caption: Self-Rewarding with length control: 22.92, 25.47, 26.93, 30.38, 34.87, 35.49. The judge gets no judge-training pairs after the initial SFT on judging data (EFT).
Meta-Rewarding: 22.92, 25.47, 27.85, 32.66, 35.45, 39.44. Judge pairs were trained in iterations 1 and 2; iterations 3 and 4 used actor pairs only.

blocks.md: Training the judge on its own meta-judgments imports new biases. By iteration 2 the meta-judge preferred the judgment with the higher score 97.68% of the time, the judge's mean score rose from 4.1 to over 4.7 out of 5, and position bias grew. Scores bunched near the top, which made responses harder to tell apart. Lesson 6 flagged the same risk: a judge's blind spots become the policy's target.

**SCoRe** (Kumar et al., 2024) trains self-correction: the model answers, is asked to find and fix any mistake without being told whether it was wrong, and answers again. Untrained, Gemini 1.5 Flash on MATH went from 52.6% to 41.4% between attempts (it broke 15.8% of problems and fixed 4.6%). Supervised fine-tuning on self-generated traces barely helped: STaR on successful revisions and Pair-SFT (pairing a wrong first answer with a correct one) gained at most 1.8 points. The causes: *distribution shift* (traces fixed the base model's mistakes, not the trained model's) and *behavior collapse* (make the best first attempt, then barely edit it). SCoRe uses on-policy multi-turn RL, first training attempt 2 while a strong KL penalty keeps attempt 1 near the base model, then training both with a progress bonus.

blocks.tex: \hat b(y_2 \mid y_1, y^{*}) = \alpha \big(\hat r(y_2, y^{*}) - \hat r(y_1, y^{*})\big), \quad \alpha > 0 \ (\text{ideally } > 1)
blocks.caption: SCoRe's bonus on the second attempt. Fixing a wrong first attempt earns +alpha; breaking a right one costs -alpha; leaving it unchanged earns 0. The rewards r come from the answer key during training.

blocks.md: On MATH, SCoRe reached 60.0% at attempt 1 and 64.4% at attempt 2, a gain of 4.4 points, while breaking only 1.4% of problems (from 15.8% for the base model). On HumanEval, with Gemini 1.0 Pro, the gain was 12.2 points. A review step helps only if it fixes more answers than it breaks; SCoRe's bonus rewards exactly that trade. Note where the signal comes from: the answer key during training. At test time no feedback is given.

Each method buys information somewhere. V-STaR gets more out of the answer key by learning from failures; SCoRe uses the answer key to reward fixes; Meta-Rewarding has no outside signal, so it can only exploit its own generation-verification gap, which Song et al. saw shrink to about zero within a few rounds on math.

blocks.question: What does V-STaR train on that STaR throws away?
options: Rationales produced with the answer given as a hint
Human-written solutions from the SFT set only
Preference labels from a stronger model
Incorrect self-generated solutions, paired with correct ones to train a DPO verifier
blocks.explain: STaR keeps only correct samples. V-STaR keeps every labeled sample in the verifier's data and builds pairs of correct and incorrect solutions to the same problem, so the verifier learns this generator's typical mistakes.

blocks.question: A model is right 90% of the time. Its self-verifier accepts 80% of correct answers and 20% of wrong ones. What is the gap, and what does it say about another round of self-improvement?
options: About 0.07: kept accuracy is 0.973, so the round can add at most about 7 points, minus distillation error
About 0.33, the same as at 30% accuracy, since the verifier did not change
0, because a verifier with 20% false positives can never help
About 0.6, because the verifier is 4 times more likely to accept a right answer
blocks.explain: Kept accuracy is 0.72 / (0.72 + 0.02) = 0.973, so the gap is 0.073. The same verifier gave 0.332 at 30% accuracy: as the generator improves there is less left to filter, one reason iterative gains saturate.

lessons.title: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop

blocks.md: Every loop so far needs a fixed set of prompts or problems. **Absolute Zero** (Zhao et al., 2025) removes that too: one model *proposes* tasks and *solves* them, and a Python executor both validates the tasks and checks the answers. It uses RLVR, as in your GRPO course, but on a curriculum the model writes for itself. A task is a triplet of program $p$, input $i$ and output $o = p(i)$. Valid tasks go into a **buffer**, a growing store of past tasks that later proposals see as examples.

blocks.title: The Absolute Zero Reasoner loop

scenes.caption: Proposer role: conditioned on a task type and K = 6 past examples from the buffer, the model writes a new program and input, asked to differ from the examples.

The executor runs it. The task is valid only if it runs and returns a value, avoids banned modules such as os.sys, sys and shutil, and returns the same output on j = 2 runs (a cheap determinism check).
The executor's output o completes the triplet (p, i, o). Hiding one part makes a task: predict o (deduction), find an input giving o (abduction), or write p from example pairs (induction).
Solver role: the same model answers. Python checks it by value equality; for abduction it checks p(guess) = p(true input), since many inputs can give the same output.
Both roles are rewarded and updated together. The only external signal is the Python executor; there is no human data beyond a trivial seed triplet (the identity function).

blocks.md: The proposer needs a reward that says which tasks are worth practicing. Absolute Zero estimates **learnability** with the solver itself: run $G$ solver rollouts on the new task (8 in their settings) and measure the average success $\bar r_{\text{solve}}$.

blocks.caption: In words: the proposer earns 0 if the solver never succeeds, otherwise 1 minus the solver's success rate; the solver earns 1 when its answer y equals the true y star. A task nobody solves teaches nothing; a task everyone solves teaches nothing. Between those, harder is better.

blocks.prompt: Four proposed tasks are solved 0, 1, 4 and 8 times out of 8 rollouts. Which earns the proposer the highest reward?
blocks.reveal: **The task solved 1 time out of 8**, with reward $1 - 1/8 = 0.875$. The 4/8 task earns 0.5, and both 0/8 and 8/8 earn 0. The reward is not centered on 50%: it favors the hardest tasks that are still within reach, the frontier where the solver has something to learn.

blocks.title: Proposer reward versus solver success over 8 rollouts

scenes.caption: The learnability reward for each possible outcome of 8 solver rollouts. Unsolvable (0/8) and trivial (8/8) tasks both earn 0.
The best task is the hardest one the solver still sometimes solves: 1/8 earns 0.875, 4/8 earns 0.5. These are also exactly the groups where GRPO gives nonzero advantages.

blocks.md: This mirrors what you know from GRPO: in a group of rollouts that all get the same reward, every advantage is zero and the group produces no gradient. Absolute Zero normalizes rewards with **Task-Relative REINFORCE++** (TRR++). REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) is the basic policy-gradient method: raise the log-probability of each sample in proportion to its reward minus a baseline. REINFORCE++ (Hu, 2025) is a variant that normalizes rewards across the whole batch instead of per question. TRR++ keeps a separate mean and standard deviation for each of the six combinations of task type and role, which the paper describes as a middle ground between GRPO's per-question baseline and one global baseline. A well-formatted wrong answer gets -0.5, and a formatting error gets -1; for the proposer, an invalid task counts as a formatting error.

blocks.caption: Each reward is centered by the mean and divided by the standard deviation of rewards for its own task type (deduction, abduction, induction) and role (propose, solve).

blocks.md: Why separate baselines? A small example with two of the six groups. Four solver answers to deduction tasks get rewards 1, 1, 1 and -0.5 (one well-formatted wrong answer). Four abduction proposals get learnability rewards 0.875, 0.5, 0 and 0.25. With one global baseline (mean 0.516, standard deviation 0.525 over all eight), the proposal worth 0.5 gets advantage -0.03: it is pushed down, only because solver rewards are larger on average. With per-group baselines (proposer mean 0.406, standard deviation 0.323) the same proposal gets +0.29, because it is better than a typical proposal. GRPO's per-question baseline would need several rollouts of the same question; TRR++ sits in between.

blocks.title: Advantages: one global baseline vs per task-and-role

scenes.caption: Global normalization (population standard deviation): 0.92, 0.92, 0.92, -1.94 for the solver; 0.69, -0.03, -0.98, -0.51 for the proposer. The decent 0.5 proposal is penalized.
Per task-and-role normalization, as in TRR++: 0.58, 0.58, 0.58, -1.73 for the solver; 1.45, 0.29, -1.26, -0.48 for the proposer. Each sample is compared with others of its own kind.

blocks.md: Results: trained from Qwen2.5 base models (Alibaba's open models, pretrained but not instruction-tuned; the coder versions had extra training on code) with no human-curated tasks, the paper reports math gains of 10.9 points (base 7B) and 15.2 points (coder 7B) on their benchmark average, compared with 0.65 for code models trained with RLVR on expert-curated code data. Gains grew with model size: +5.7, +10.2 and +13.2 overall for 3B, 7B and 14B coder models. They also report an "uh-oh moment": with Llama 3.1 8B, the model occasionally wrote concerning chains of thought, which they flag for safety work.

"Zero data" does not mean zero prior knowledge. The model is a pretrained LLM, and the coder base model, which started 3.6 points lower in math, ended 0.7 points above the general base. The executor is the external signal; it can only certify what running deterministic Python can check.

Now compare the whole family by asking where the signal comes from and what caps it:

- **AlphaZero**: search plus exact game outcomes. Capped by search and network capacity, not by data.
- **STaR, ReST-EM**: an answer key or unit tests. Capped by the problem set and by lucky false positives.
- **ReST**: a learned reward model. Capped by how faithful that proxy is.
- **SPIN**: the human SFT responses. Capped by the data distribution itself.
- **Self-Rewarding**: the model's own judgment. Capped by the judge, with risk of reward hacking.
- **Absolute Zero**: a code executor. Capped by what execution can verify.

Lesson 9 adds adversarial self-play and AlphaProof to this list.

For any self-improvement claim, ask two questions: what outside the current model decides that a sample is good, and how often is it wrong? The loop can only improve as far as that signal is informative.

blocks.question: An Absolute Zero proposer writes a program that calls random.random() and returns the result. What happens to this proposal?
options: It becomes a hard abduction task, so the proposer gets a high learnability reward
It fails validation (random is a forbidden module, and two runs would give different outputs anyway), so it counts as a formatting error with reward -1
The solver gets credit for any numeric answer between 0 and 1
It is accepted, but only as an induction task
blocks.explain: Absolute Zero only accepts deterministic programs: it bans modules such as random and datetime outright, and it also runs each program twice (j = 2) and compares outputs. Only proposals that produce valid triplets count as correctly formatted, so this one gets the -1 penalty, which teaches the proposer to avoid unverifiable tasks.

blocks.question: A team wants a model to improve its customer-support replies, has thousands of real customer questions, and has no answer key or human preference labels. Which loop fits, and what is the main risk to monitor?
options: ReST-EM with a binary correctness reward; the risk is overfitting a small problem set
AlphaZero-style tree search; the risk is lack of exploration noise
Absolute Zero; the risk is nondeterministic programs
Self-Rewarding with the model as judge; the risk is the policy exploiting the judge, for example by growing longer replies
blocks.explain: Without checkable answers, the options are a judge or a human target. Self-Rewarding needs only prompts and a seed of judging examples. Its documented risk is that the judge's biases get amplified: the paper itself saw average response length grow about 2.3x over two iterations and flagged reward hacking.

lessons.title: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof

blocks.md: AlphaZero's loop needs two things: an opponent that improves as fast as you do, and rules that score the game for free. Can a language model get both? Take the word game **Adversarial Taboo**. An attacker secretly holds a target word, say *conversation*, and chats with a defender. The attacker wins if the defender says the word without noticing; the defender wins by announcing a correct guess, and loses with a wrong one. Nobody needs a judge model: a string check decides every game.

**SPAG** (Cheng et al., 2024) has one LLM play both roles through two prompts, so it plays against a copy of itself. The game is zero-sum: the attacker's total reward is the negative of the defender's. Before self-play the model first imitates game episodes played by GPT-4, because open models did not follow the rules reliably, so the loop does not start from zero outside data. Then each epoch collects self-play episodes (at most 5 turns, target words from a list of frequent English words), keeps the winning side's episodes, ReST-style, and trains with an offline policy-gradient loss, mixed with Alpaca instruction data to keep general skills.

blocks.title: One Adversarial Taboo episode (target: conversation)

scenes.caption: Only the attacker sees the target word. Both players are the same LLM under different prompts.
The defender must keep talking without ever producing the target word by accident.
The defender may guess at any time. A correct guess wins for the defender; a wrong guess or an accidental use of the word wins for the attacker; 5 turns with neither is a tie.
A string check scores the game: +1 for one side, -1 for the other. Winning episodes become training data for that role.

blocks.md: On LLaMA-2-7B the geometric mean over eight benchmarks (seven reasoning sets such as BBH and ARC, plus MMLU for general knowledge) went from 50.22 after imitation to 51.69, 52.19 and 52.58 after three SPAG epochs, ahead of continued instruction tuning of the imitation model (51.20). The gains are small but consistent; general knowledge (MMLU) did not always rise, and for Baichuan-2-13B it dipped slightly. Self-play on a non-adversarial word game with a narrow topic range (Guess My City) even did worse than imitation alone.

**SPIRAL** (Liu et al., 2025) makes it fully online and multi-turn: one shared policy plays both seats of TicTacToe, Kuhn Poker (a 3-card poker game) and Simple Negotiation, with no expert data, and is updated with REINFORCE on the game outcome. The problem with one policy in two roles: the roles have different typical returns (the first player in TicTacToe has an advantage; poker players see different cards), so raw outcomes mostly measure the seat, not the move. SPIRAL's **role-conditioned advantage estimation** (RAE) keeps a separate baseline for each game and role, updated as a moving average.

blocks.tex: b_{G,p} \leftarrow \alpha\, b_{G,p} + (1-\alpha)\, R_p(\tau), \qquad A_{G,p}(\tau) = R_p(\tau) - b_{G,p}
blocks.caption: G is the game, p in {0, 1} the seat, R_p the return of the episode for that seat, alpha a decay rate in [0, 1]. Each action of player p is weighted by A_{G,p}, so a win from the favored seat counts less than a win from the hard seat.

blocks.md: This is the same idea as Absolute Zero's TRR++ in lesson 8, which keeps one baseline per task type and role. Without RAE, SPIRAL's models suffered what the paper calls *thinking collapse*: reasoning traces shrank from about 2,000 characters to almost nothing and outputs degenerated to strings like `\boxed{bet}`, while benchmark scores fell. With it, multi-game training raised Qwen3-4B-Base's average on 8 reasoning benchmarks from 34.0% to 44.5% and Qwen3-8B-Base's from 39.5% to 49.6%, better than supervised fine-tuning on 25,000 expert game trajectories, and better than RL against fixed opponents, which the model learns to exploit.

**R-Zero** (Huang et al., 2025) splits one base model into two models: a **Challenger** that writes math questions and a **Solver** that answers them, trained in alternation with GRPO. For each question the Solver samples $m = 10$ answers; the most common one becomes the **pseudo-label**, and $\hat p$ is the share of answers that agree with it. The Challenger is rewarded for questions where the Solver is maximally unsure, minus a penalty for questions that are near-duplicates (BLEU, a word-overlap score from machine translation) of others in the batch. The Solver trains only on questions where 3 to 7 of its 10 answers match the pseudo-label, with reward 1 for matching it.

blocks.caption: R-Zero rewards agreement near one half with its own majority vote; Absolute Zero (lesson 8) rewards a low but nonzero success rate measured by a Python executor.

blocks.title: Proposer rewards over 10 solver answers

scenes.caption: R-Zero: x/10 answers agree with the majority (at least 1 always does). Reward peaks at 5/10 (1.0) and is 0 at 10/10. Bars in the band 3/10 to 7/10 are also the questions the Solver may train on.
Absolute Zero's rule for comparison, reading x/10 as the true solve rate: 0.9 at 1/10 down to 0 at 10/10. It favors the hardest solvable tasks; R-Zero favors maximal disagreement.

blocks.prompt: R-Zero has no answer key and no code executor. Its Solver is rewarded for matching its own majority vote. What would you expect to happen to the accuracy of those pseudo-labels as the Challenger learns to write harder questions?
blocks.reveal: **It falls.** The authors had GPT-4o answer 200 sampled questions per iteration as a reference: pseudo-label accuracy was 79% after the first iteration, 69% after the second and 63% after the third. Harder questions are exactly where a majority vote is wrong more often, so the Solver is increasingly trained toward wrong answers.

blocks.md: R-Zero raised Qwen3-4B-Base's math average by 6.49 points after three iterations. But it does not keep going: performance peaked and then fell for every model size, after the first iteration for Qwen3-0.6B-Base and after the third for Qwen3-4B-Base. The authors find falling labels are not the whole story: the 0.6B model began to decline with labels still 70.6% accurate while the 4B model kept improving at 48.8%, and they point to model collapse from training only on self-made data, the prerequisite course's setting. The split into two models does help: one shared model in both roles peaked after a single iteration and had less accurate labels (63.4% versus 71.0%). Compare Absolute Zero: there the executor checks every answer exactly, so harder tasks never mean noisier labels.

**AlphaProof** (Hubert et al., Nature 2025) is AlphaZero with a theorem prover as the game. In Lean, a proof assistant, the state is the current list of hypotheses and goals and an action is a **tactic**, a small program that advances the proof one step. Lean's kernel checks every step, so a finished proof is certainly correct: the exact judge. Each tactic costs a reward of -1, so shorter proofs score higher; when a goal splits into subgoals that must all be proved, the search uses an AND-OR tree and the return is that of the hardest subgoal. A 3-billion-parameter proof network outputs tactics (the policy) and a value, and guides a tree search as in lesson 2.

blocks.title: AlphaProof: AlphaZero with Lean as the rules

nodes.label:
Tree search guided
by proof network

Lean kernel checks
proof or disproof

scenes.caption: A curriculum is needed because, unlike Go, proving has no single start position. An auto-formalizer turned about 1 million problems into about 80 million Lean statements; even an unfaithful translation is a valid problem to prove or disprove.
Distributed actors attempt each statement with tree search, sending tactics to Lean. Proofs and disproofs that Lean accepts are the only success signal.

The verified experience trains the proof network, which guides the next searches: the AlphaZero loop. The main RL phase used about 80,000 TPU days (TPUs are Google's machine learning accelerator chips).
Test-time RL: for one hard target, generate variants (simplifications, generalizations) and run the same loop on them, adapting the network to that problem before attacking it again.

blocks.md: Before RL the network was pretrained on about 300 billion tokens of code and math and fine-tuned on about 300,000 state-tactic pairs from Mathlib, Lean's community math library. At the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, experts formalized the five non-geometry problems; for problems that ask to find an answer, Gemini proposed hundreds of candidates and AlphaProof refuted most of the wrong ones (99% for P1, but only 7% for P6). With 2 to 3 days of test-time RL each, AlphaProof proved P1, P2 and P6 (the hardest, solved by five human contestants); with AlphaGeometry 2 solving P4, the system scored 28 of 42, in the silver-medal range. On historical IMO and Putnam benchmarks, test-time RL added about 15 points over 12 TPU hours of search alone.

A conceptual sibling with no exact judge at all: **Iterated Amplification** (Christiano et al., 2018). A human $H$ answers a question by splitting it into subquestions, asking copies of the current model $X$ to answer them, and combining the answers; the model is trained to imitate this amplified system, $\text{Amplify}_H(X)$. The authors describe it as Expert Iteration without an external reward function: the training signal comes only from how the human decomposes and combines, which is the same improve-then-distill shape as lesson 1.

Extending lesson 8's list of where the signal comes from and what caps it:

- **SPAG**: a string rule scores the game; starts by imitating GPT-4. Capped by what the game exercises.
- **SPIRAL**: game rules, opponent improves with you. Capped by how far game skills transfer.
- **R-Zero**: the Solver's own majority vote. Capped by pseudo-label accuracy, which falls as questions harden, and by collapse from training only on its own questions.
- **AlphaProof**: the Lean kernel, exact. Capped by search, compute and what can be formalized.
- **Iterated Amplification**: human decomposition. Capped by how well tasks decompose.

Adversarial self-play gives an automatic curriculum, an opponent or proposer that keeps the task at the edge of ability. It does not by itself create a correct signal. The strongest results, from AlphaZero to AlphaProof, pair self-play with a judge that is never wrong.

blocks.question: In R-Zero, the Solver answers a new question 10 times. Which outcome puts the question in the Solver's training set?
options: 10 of 10 answers agree, so the label is surely right
1 of 10 agree, the hardest kind of question
5 of 10 agree, inside the 3 to 7 band
Any outcome, as long as a Python executor validates the question
blocks.explain: R-Zero keeps a question only if 3 to 7 of the 10 answers match the majority-vote pseudo-label: not trivially easy, and not so uncertain that the majority answer is likely to be wrong. There is no executor; the label is the model's own vote.

blocks.question: SPIRAL trains one policy for both seats of TicTacToe with REINFORCE. Why does a single global baseline give misleading advantages?
options: The two seats have different expected returns (first-move advantage), so a global baseline credits the seat instead of the moves
A global baseline has higher variance only for single-player games
REINFORCE cannot use any baseline in multi-agent settings
The global baseline makes the game no longer zero-sum
blocks.explain: If the first player wins more often, a global baseline makes nearly every first-player move look good and every second-player move look bad. RAE subtracts a separate running mean per game and seat, so only better-than-usual play for that seat is reinforced.

blocks.question: AlphaProof's training problems come from an auto-formalizer that sometimes mistranslates the original problem. Why does this not corrupt the training signal?
options: Mistranslated statements are removed by a human reviewer
Any Lean statement is a real problem: Lean checks whatever proof or disproof is found, so each attempt is labeled correctly even if it is not the intended problem
The value head learns to ignore mistranslated problems
Test-time RL replaces the main RL data
blocks.explain: The paper notes that each auto-formalized statement, faithful or not, is a valid formal problem to prove or disprove. The judge, Lean's kernel, is exact about the statement actually given, so the experience is always correctly labeled.
